tldr: By integrating exteroception (elevation map) and proprioception using an attention-based recurrent encoder, this quadruped controller automatically falls back to proprioception when facing sensor noise or misleading visual data. It tackled challenging Alpine mountain trails at human-like speeds with zero falls.
hero_caption: Validation experiments conducted across diverse real-world environments through all four seasons, including forests, snowy mountains, steep slopes, underground tunnels, and urban stairs. The robot traversed multiple complex hazards—such as slippery surfaces, invisible obstacles, and deep snow—without falling even once.
overview:
For quadrupedal robots to move quickly across unknown rough terrain, exteroceptive perception is essential. It lets the robot look at the terrain ahead and adjust its gait before making contact with the ground. In real field conditions, however, visual information frequently fails due to soft materials like snow and grass, reflections from puddles, sensor overexposure, occlusions, and odometry drift. Because of this, most conventional robust controllers fell back on relying purely on proprioception—blindly feeling out the ground with tactile sensations at the feet and joint states. While safe, this severely limits locomotion speed.

To address this, the authors propose an end-to-end learning framework that seamlessly combines the speed of exteroception with the robustness of proprioception. At its core is a recurrent (GRU) belief state encoder equipped with an attention mechanism. When exteroception is reliable, the system leverages ahead-of-time terrain information to speed up locomotion. When the visual data is corrupted or missing, it automatically down-weights the exteroceptive input and falls back to a proprioception-driven gait.

For evaluation, the robot tackled a hiking trail on Mount Etzel in the Swiss Alps, featuring a 120 m elevation gain over 2.2 km (difficulty rating: difficult). It reached the summit in 31 minutes, beating the official estimated time for human hikers (35 minutes), and completed the 78-minute round trip with zero falls and zero human assistance. This landmark achievement overcomes perception failures without heuristics, delivering animal-like agile and robust locomotion.
contributions: Proposed a belief state encoder that integrates exteroception (elevation maps) and proprioception using a GRU and a gating mechanism (attention), adaptively adjusting reliance on exteroceptive data based on noise levels.

Bridged the sim-to-real gap for zero-shot real-world transfer by distilling knowledge (privileged learning) from an omniscient privileged teacher to a student operating only on noisy partial observations.
Demonstrated high robustness with zero falls and high-speed locomotion across diverse seasons and extreme environments, including an hour-long hike in the Alps and the DARPA Subterranean Challenge.

sections.heading: Why robots cannot always trust their eyes on natural trails
sections.summary: While vision is crucial for fast locomotion across rugged terrain, real-world depth sensing is riddled with noise and dropouts that can cause controllers to fail. This work aims to establish robust locomotion immune to perceptual failures by developing a learning-based belief encoder that integrates vision and proprioception.
sections.details:
Quadrupedal robots capable of traversing hazardous environments that humans cannot enter—such as disaster zones and planetary surfaces—are in high demand. Animals like humans and dogs naturally combine exteroception (what they see) with proprioception (muscles and joints) to run smoothly across irregular terrain without tripping.

Replicating this on a robot has proven extremely difficult, primarily due to the uncertainty of onboard depth sensors:
- Stereo cameras lose disparity on textureless walls, snow, or under harsh lighting contrasts.
- Time-of-flight (ToF) cameras suffer from high noise in direct sunlight and cannot measure dark surfaces.
- In 2.5D elevation maps, soft ground like vegetation or snow cannot be distinguished from solid ground, and overhangs such as tree branches are falsely mapped as impassable obstacles.
- Foot slippage corrupts robot odometry, causing massive distortion throughout the map.

To avoid these perceptual pitfalls, conventional model predictive control (MPC) and reinforcement learning approaches typically either relied on pre-scanned accurate maps, or completely blinded themselves outdoors to walk using "proprioception only." However, because the robot cannot notice an obstacle until its foot physically collides with it, locomotion speed had to be drastically reduced.

This paper aims to get the best of both worlds. The authors present an end-to-end integrated controller requiring no heuristics: it takes wide, fast strides by planning ahead when vision is reliable, and seamlessly switches to proprioceptive stepping as soon as vision is compromised.

sections.heading: Hiking the Alps at human speeds without stopping when vision fails
sections.summary: Extensive real-world experiments on the ANYmal platform showed it could complete a challenging Alpine trail in a time comparable to or faster than human hikers. Furthermore, the robot updated its internal belief state appropriately to keep walking even when confronted with transparent obstacles, soft sponges, or blinded sensors.
sections.details:
Using the ANYmal C quadruped robot, the team performed extensive traversal experiments ranging from urban settings to wild nature and underground spaces.

### Fast and robust locomotion in the wild
Traversal was tested across forests, rocky terrain, muddy paths, snowy trails, and underground tunnels. Stair climbing was particularly noteworthy. Commercial quadrupeds such as Boston Dynamics' Spot require switching to a dedicated stair mode and aligning squarely with the steps. In contrast, this approach needs no mode switching at all: the robot can climb and descend forward, diagonally, sideways, and even turn mid-staircase smoothly. It achieved zero falls even on snow-covered, slippery stairs where sensor overexposure caused missing elevation maps.

### A hike in the Alps
To test the limits of the controller, a hiking experiment was conducted on Mount Etzel in Switzerland, featuring a 120 m elevation change over 2.2 km with slopes up to 38% (Fig. F2). The route is officially rated as "difficult" in hiking guides. Navigating rocks, tree roots, and wet, steep slopes, ANYmal recorded an ascent time of 31 minutes. This was 4 minutes faster than the human hiking estimate on the official trail signpost (35 minutes). It completed the entire round trip in 78 minutes (compared to the hiking planner's suggested 76 minutes) without a single fall or human intervention, except for a scheduled battery swap and shoe reattachment.

### Exteroceptive challenges
As shown in Fig. F3, the controller was evaluated against common real-world perception failures: map dropouts from reflective metal grating (B) and snow (C), misclassified overhead brush and tall grass (D, E), map distortion from foot slippage (F), and occlusions on steep inclines (G). Across all these adversarial conditions, locomotion remained stable, gracefully falling back to proprioception.

### Evaluating the contribution of exteroception
A quantitative comparison was made against a proprioceptive-only baseline (Fig. F4):
- For clearing a single high step, the baseline's success rate dropped sharply at 20 cm as its front feet caught the edge, whereas the proposed method reliably cleared obstacles up to 30.5 cm. It naturally learned adaptive motions: spotting the step in advance, lifting the front legs high, and pitching the body forward to let the hind legs clear.
- In an obstacle course, the baseline took 75 seconds and got stuck in three spots, requiring human pushes to recover. The proposed method cleared it autonomously in 33 seconds.
- Flat-ground walking speed reached 1.2 m/s (2x the baseline's 0.6 m/s), and turning speed reached 3.0 rad/s (5x the baseline's 0.6 rad/s).

### Evaluating robustness with belief state visualization
The internal belief state of the controller was visualized during perception failures (Fig. F5):
- When stepping on a soft sponge (A), the robot initially relies on vision to place its foot. The moment the foot sinks in, the internal elevation estimate (blue dots) is quickly corrected downward, and the GRU's memory maintains this estimate even after the foot lifts off.
- On a transparent acrylic step (B), which is invisible to depth sensors, the robot initially steps as if on flat ground. Upon foot contact, it detects the step instantly and corrects its gait.
- When the sensors were completely covered with a cloth during stair climbing (C, D), the robot recognized the staircase the instant its foot made contact with the first step and ascended stably.

captions.F2: The hiking route and field conditions on Mount Etzel, Switzerland. Over a demanding 2.2 km trail with slopes up to 38% over rocks and wet inclines, the robot reached the summit in 31 minutes—faster than the official human walking estimate (35 minutes).
captions.F3: Examples of exteroceptive perception failures in real environments: reflections on metal grating (B), depth dropouts on snow (C), overhead foliage (D), soft grass (E), map distortion caused by foot slippage (F), and blind spots/occlusions (G). The robot traversed all of them without falling despite misleading maps.
captions.F4: Quantitative comparison with and without exteroception. While the baseline failed at single steps over 20 cm (A, B), the proposed method overcame steps up to 30.5 cm. Substantial performance gains were also seen on the obstacle course (C, D) and in maximum speeds (E–H).

On soft foam (A), transparent steps (B), and complete visual occlusion (D), the internal estimate swiftly adjusts toward ground truth upon foot contact.

sections.heading: The core technology behind DARPA SubT victory and future challenges
sections.summary: This work presents the first rough-terrain quadruped locomotion controller that combines the speed of vision with the robustness of proprioception. Deployed as the standard locomotion controller for the winning team at the DARPA Subterranean Challenge, it powered over 1,700 m of underground exploration without a single fall. Future directions include explicitly modeling uncertainty and processing raw sensor inputs directly.
sections.details:
The controller's extreme robustness was proven under competitive pressure. In the DARPA Subterranean Challenge Final Event—a contest focused on autonomous exploration in hazardous underground environments—it served as the default locomotion controller for the winning Team Cerberus. Across tunnels and caves filled with smoke, dust, muddy water, and complete darkness, four ANYmal robots traversed a combined distance of more than 1,700 m with zero falls, playing a decisive role in the team's victory.

Nevertheless, several opportunities for improvement and limitations remain:
- **Explicit handling of uncertainty**: The current policy handles terrain uncertainty only implicitly. If there is an occlusion near a cliff or a stepping stone, the robot might assume ground exists and step into empty space. Explicitly estimating uncertainty could enable smarter behaviors, such as extending a leg to cautiously probe for contact on uncertain footing.
- **Moving beyond elevation maps**: The pipeline currently builds an intermediate 2.5D elevation map from raw point clouds. While this provides sensor-agnostic flexibility (working with both LiDAR and depth cameras without retraining), it discards valuable visual cues like ground material, friction, and texture. Furthermore, odometry drift directly degrades map quality, motivating future end-to-end architectures that integrate raw sensor streams directly.
- **Extreme or acrobatic maneuvers**: The controller does not cover motions outside normal gait patterns, such as extricating a leg trapped in a narrow hole or chimneying up steep, vertical ledges.

sections.heading: How privileged learning and attention-gated GRUs estimate belief
sections.summary: A teacher policy with privileged information (friction, true terrain) was trained via reinforcement learning in a physics simulator, and then distilled into a student policy operating on noisy observations available on the real robot. The student network incorporates an attention-gated recurrent encoder that dynamically evaluates the reliability of exteroceptive input.
sections.details:
The complete training and deployment pipeline consists of three main stages (Fig. F6).

### 1. Privileged Teacher Training
Using the RaiSim physics simulator, an omniscient teacher policy is trained via Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO):
- **Observations**: In addition to proprioception $o_t^p$ (joint angles, angular velocities) and true terrain elevation around the feet $o_t^e$, the teacher receives privileged information $s_t^p$ (contact forces, contact normals, friction coefficients, foot collision states, and external perturbation forces).
- **Action Space**: Inspired by Central Pattern Generators (CPGs), actions are parameterized as phase offsets $\varDelta\phi_l$ and residual target joint angles $\varDelta q_i$ relative to nominal leg trajectories tied to leg phases $\phi_l$.
- **Reward and Curriculum**: Rewards incentivize target velocity tracking, posture maintenance, and smoothness (penalizing joint torques and accelerations). Terrain difficulty is scaled progressively using a particle-filter-based curriculum.

### 2. Student Policy Training and Belief Encoder
Next, a student policy that uses only partial observations available on the physical robot is trained to reproduce the teacher's behavior via imitation learning:
- **Severe Noise Model**: To simulate real-world perception failures, elevation samples are perturbed with Gaussian noise controlled by an 8-dimensional parameter $z$, covering horizontal shifts, height perturbations, leg-wise offsets, and long-term drift (Fig. F7A, B). Noise regimes are randomized across standard noise (60%), large offsets (30%), and complete sensor dropouts (10%).
- **Gated Belief Encoder**: A GRU with hidden state $h_t$ synthesizes a latent belief vector $b_t$ from the historical time series (Fig. F7C). Crucially, a gating mechanism uses an attention vector $\alpha = \sigma(g_a(b_t'))$. By computing the Hadamard product $\alpha \odot g_b(l_t^e)$ with exteroceptive features $l_t^e$, the network shuts out visual information whenever it is deemed untrustworthy, falling back to proprioception.
- **Loss Function**: The student minimizes a combination of behavior cloning loss (matching teacher actions) and reconstruction loss (reconstructing privileged states and true terrain elevations from the belief state).

### 3. Deployment
The trained student policy transfers zero-shot to the physical ANYmal without any fine-tuning. A GPU-accelerated Kalman-filter-based 2.5D elevation mapping pipeline operates at 20 Hz, from which terrain height around the feet is sampled and fed to the policy at 50 Hz. Because the elevation map serves as an abstraction layer, the identical policy runs seamlessly on robots equipped with LiDAR or RealSense depth cameras without retraining.

captions.F6: Overall architecture of the approach: (1) Privileged teacher training using PPO in simulation, (2) distillation into a student policy that estimates belief states from noisy inputs via imitation learning, and (3) zero-shot deployment to the physical robot without fine-tuning.
captions.F7: Detailed design for robust perception: (A, B) multi-level noise model adding point-wise, leg-wise, and episode-wise corruption during student training; (C) belief encoder architecture using a GRU and a sigmoid attention gate to dynamically suppress vision inputs based on reliability.

takeaways: Instead of choosing between 'vision-reliant MPC' and 'vision-blind proprioceptive RL', an attention-gated belief state architecture dynamically evaluates perceptual reliability and enables seamless fallback.

Injecting harsh simulation noise encompassing real-world failure modes—point-level jitter, leg-wise offsets, and complete map dropouts—yields real-world resilience against sensor overexposure and foot slippage.
Using an elevation map as an abstraction layer allows the exact same trained policy to be deployed interchangeably across different sensor setups (e.g., LiDAR vs. stereo cameras) without retraining.
limitations: Relying on a 2.5D elevation map as an intermediate representation discards rich sensory signals like surface texture, color, and direct visual friction cues.
Odometry is handled by an independent upstream module; if odometry fails completely, the resulting map distortions can adversely impact locomotion performance.
Because uncertainty in blind spots (occlusions) is not explicitly modeled, the robot risks stepping into empty air on discontinuous drop-offs or stepping stones.
